nature-eco-763.title: How many people can the Earth sustain?
nature-eco-763.text: Nobody agrees on how many people the Earth can sustain. A sustainable population is a proposed number of humans that the planet, or a region such as a nation or continent, could support over time. It is the human case of {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. A 2004 meta-analysis of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion, ranging from 0.65 to 9.8 billion. Recent estimates that weigh climate change, nutrient loading and biodiversity loss are lower, between 2 and 4 billion. Paul Ehrlich put the optimum at 1.5 to 2 billion in 2018. Sceptics dispute the assumptions behind such figures, and they note that the countries driving unsustainable consumption tend to be richer, with slower population growth.

nature-eco-762.title: Earth system science: treating the planet as one system
nature-eco-762.text: Earth system science asks what happens when you study the whole planet as a single, interacting system. It applies systems science to the Earth, studying feedbacks between its spheres and the impact of human societies. It draws on natural and social sciences, including ecology and economics, and takes a holistic view. Its four named features of the Earth System are variability, life, connectivity and non-linearity. Because of strong non-linearities, a small change in a forcing function can push the system across a threshold and cause abrupt change. The field grew partly from a NASA committee formed in 1983, whose reports in 1986 and 1988 stressed human impacts as the reason to join the life and geosciences. It treats the {{ref:nature-found-022}} as part of a {{ref:nature-eco-621}}.

nature-eco-727.title: Methane: the gas that warms fast
nature-eco-727.text: One tonne of leaked methane warms the planet as much as 82.5 tonnes of carbon dioxide over 20 years. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon, a molecule with four equivalent C-H bonds, and the main component of natural gas, which is about 87% methane by volume. Burned, it releases less carbon dioxide per unit of heat than other hydrocarbon fuels, and it can be shipped as refrigerated liquefied natural gas. It is also a {{ref:nature-eco-162}}, responsible for around 30% of the rise in global temperatures since the industrial revolution. Its warming potential is 29.8 times that of carbon dioxide over 100 years. Another source gives 25 for that period. Its atmospheric concentration rose from 722 ppb before industry to 1936 ppb by 2025. Steam reforming of natural gas is also the standard industrial source of hydrogen, with over 50 million tonnes made yearly in 2013.

nature-eco-682.title: Sediment: loose material carried somewhere new
nature-eco-682.text: A riverbank, a beach and a sandstone cliff share one origin: sediment. It is solid material made of loose particles that has been transported to a new place and deposited. Weathering and erosion break material down, and then wind, water, ice or gravity carry it away. Most sediment moves by water, in what are called fluvial processes, but wind carries some, called aeolian sediment, and glaciers carry more. Moraines and till are ice-borne sediments. Scientists classify it by grain size, grain shape and composition, and measure size on the log base 2 Phi scale from colloid to boulder. Buried sand and silt can become sandstone and siltstone through lithification, so deposited sediment is the source of sedimentary rocks.

nature-eco-717.title: Hydrology: following water through the Earth
nature-eco-717.text: Water on Earth never stays put, and hydrology is the study of where it goes. It is the scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth and other planets. Its central theme is that water circulates through the Earth by different pathways at different rates, as in the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}. Hydrologists collect and analyse data to solve problems such as environmental preservation, natural disasters and water management. The field divides into surface water hydrology, groundwater hydrology (hydrogeology) and marine hydrology. Applications include calculating runoff and precipitation, determining regional and agricultural water balance, designing riparian restoration, and predicting flood, landslide and drought risk. The need is old: ancient Egyptians used basin irrigation, and Mesopotamian towns were protected from floods by high earthen walls.

nature-eco-711.title: Economic development: improving lives, not only output
nature-eco-711.text: Is a richer country always a better-off one? Economic development is the process by which the economic well-being and quality of life of a nation, region, community or individual are improved. It differs from {{ref:nature-econ-478}}: development is a policy intervention to improve well-being, whereas growth is a market phenomenon of rising productivity and output. Policies historically focused on industrialization and infrastructure, and since the 1960s on poverty reduction. In 1997 the UNDP defined development as increasing people's choices, naming empowerment, equity, productivity and sustainability as chief factors. One flaw is that GDP per capita is calculated without deducting depreciation of fabricated assets or depletion and degradation of natural resources. The state's capabilities most often limit a country's goals, so a gradual approach avoids burdensome ones. The definition is itself contested: 20th-century economists stressed growth, while sociologists stress other aspects.

nature-eco-687.title: The benthic zone: life on the bottom
nature-eco-687.text: The benthic zone is the lowest ecological region of a body of water, including the sediment surface and some sub-surface layers. It applies to streams, rivers, lakes and oceans. In the ocean it starts at the shoreline and runs out over the continental shelf. The shelf edge is usually about 200 metres deep, and the generally flat abyssal plain is usually about 4,000 metres deep. Ocean habitats are zoned by depth into epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathyal, abyssal and hadal. Human impacts occur at all depths but are most significant on shallow continental shelf and slope habitats, where the bottom lies nearest to people. Its floor is made of {{ref:nature-eco-682}}.

nature-eco-742.title: The water table: where the ground turns wet
nature-eco-742.text:
Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the ground turns wet. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation, below which ground pores are filled with groundwater. Above it lies the vadose zone. Below it, permeable rock layers that yield groundwater are aquifers. It is not the same as the water level in a confined deeper aquifer, which is the potentiometric surface. The table rises and falls seasonally with precipitation and evapotranspiration, and where it reaches the surface, springs, rivers, lakes and oases occur. Groundwater entering rivers and lakes supplies their base-flow water levels.

People change it. Fossil water, held for millennia mainly in deserts, is not renewed by rainfall, so extraction permanently changes the table. Crops need a minimum depth: cotton in the Nile Delta is sensitive and needs a deep table, while wheat tolerates 45 cm. Near the coast, lower tables from heavier water use have let seawater contaminate groundwater, as in Libya and Israel.

nature-eco-678.title: Permafrost: frozen ground that is starting to thaw
nature-eco-678.text:
Under the Arctic lies a freezer holding more carbon than anyone wants released. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays below 0 degrees C continuously for two years or more. It lies beneath an active layer that freezes and thaws each year and supports plant growth. Its depth ranges from under a metre to 1,493 m in the Lena and Yana basins of Siberia. It is discontinuous where mean annual soil surface temperature is between -5 and 0 degrees C, and subsea permafrost lies on polar continental shelves. Only shallow-rooted plants survive on it, and black spruce dominates where it is extensive. Ice-rich thaw creates thermokarst landforms such as thermokarst lakes, thaw slumps and gullies.

The ground is warming: permafrost warmed about 0.3 degrees C globally between 2007 and 2016. That deepens the active layer and releases stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, a positive climate feedback sometimes counted as a tipping point. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates permafrost emissions could equal 14-175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per degree of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of annual human emissions by 2019. People are exposed too. As of 2021, 1162 Arctic settlements with about 5 million people sit on permafrost, and the ground under 42% of them is expected to thaw by 2050. Deep permafrost was once used for hazardous waste, and about 4500 Arctic industrial facilities process or store hazardous chemicals there as of 2023.

nature-eco-709.title: Detritus: the dead matter that feeds the living
nature-eco-709.text: Most of the living world runs on the dead. Detritus is organic matter made of the decomposing remains of organisms, plant material and faeces. It hosts microorganisms that colonise and remineralise it, such as decomposers, detritivores and coprophages. On land it is plant litter mixed with soil as soil organic matter. In freshwater it is mostly leaf litter, and in marine systems it is suspended organic matter that settles as marine snow. On land, far more dead material is broken down through the detritus chain than is eaten alive by animals. Most freshwater detritus comes from nearby land, and plant litter is the main carbon source in small-order streams.

nature-eco-703.title: Deserts: dry land that covers a third of Earth
nature-eco-703.text: About one third of Earth's land surface is arid or semi-arid, including much of the polar regions, sometimes called cold deserts. A desert is a landscape with little precipitation, whose dry conditions support distinctive biomes and ecosystems. Deserts generally get less than 250 mm a year. Semi-deserts get 250-500 mm, and grass-clad ones are steppes. Clear skies let heat radiate away at night, so daily temperature ranges can reach 20 to 30 degC. Contrary to the postcard image, around 20% of desert is sand, from 2% in North America to 30% in Australia and over 45% in Central Asia. Plant growth is limited by rainfall, temperature extremes and desiccating winds, so biomass and primary productivity are low. Deserts support only a limited human and animal population, and are exploited for minerals and solar energy.

nature-eco-681.title: Savanna: grassland with scattered trees
nature-eco-681.text:
A savanna is a mixed woodland-grassland biome whose trees are spaced widely enough that the canopy does not close. The open canopy lets light reach an unbroken grass layer. Savannas have seasonal water, with most rain in one season, and often lie between forest and desert or grassland. Year-to-year rainfall variation and dry-season wildfires are common to all of them.

Fire shaped many savannas. Fire-stick farming appears to explain much of the savanna in tropical Australia and New Guinea, and Indian savannas result from human fire use. Fires kill or suppress tree seedlings and keep the canopy open. Today less than three percent of savanna ecosystems are estimated to be highly intact. Grazing by livestock changes pasture and promotes woody plant encroachment, since removing grass cuts competition for water and removes fuel that would feed fires. Clearing trees for pasture can raise production two- to fourfold, and about 4,800 km2 of Queensland savanna was cleared annually in the 2000s. Introduced weeds such as buffel grass and prickly acacia can alter savanna structure and composition worldwide.

nature-eco-014.title: Climate change feedbacks: loops that speed or slow warming
nature-eco-014.text:
Emissions are only half the story of warming. Climate change feedbacks are natural processes that change how much global temperature rises for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. Emissions are the forcing, and feedbacks combine to set climate sensitivity to that forcing. The overall sum of feedbacks is negative but becoming less negative as emissions continue, so warming is slower than it would be without feedbacks, yet will accelerate if emissions continue.

Warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas, forming a positive loop that continues until negative feedbacks restore equilibrium. Lapse rate feedback is generally negative but positive in polar regions, where it strongly contributed to polar amplified warming. Low clouds cool strongly while thin high clouds warm, and climate change is expected to reduce clouds' overall cooling, a clear positive feedback globally. The ocean absorbs about one third of current emissions through the solubility pump, and ultimately about 75% of emitted CO2 will dissolve in the ocean over centuries. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates permafrost could release CO2 and methane equal to 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 degC of warming. Uncertainty over carbon cycle feedbacks may affect emission reduction targets, since concentration and temperature targets both need future carbon cycle changes.

nature-eco-689.title: Bioaccumulation: how poisons build up in a body
nature-eco-689.text:
A chemical present at low levels in the environment can still poison an animal slowly. Bioaccumulation is the gradual build-up of substances such as pesticides or other chemicals in an organism. It occurs when an organism takes in a substance faster than it can lose it by catabolism and excretion. The longer a toxic substance's biological half-life, the greater the risk of chronic poisoning, even when environmental levels are low.

Two related ideas help. Bioconcentration is a higher chemical concentration inside an organism than in the surrounding air or water. Biotransformation, the body's chemical alteration of a substance, can strongly change how much of it accumulates. Because the build-up matters at each step of the {{ref:nature-eco-305}} chain, understanding bioaccumulation helps in the assessment and control of chemicals and their use.

nature-eco-699.title: Controlled burns: fighting fire with fire
nature-eco-699.text: Managers sometimes light fires on purpose. A controlled or prescribed burn is a fire set deliberately to remove built-up vegetation and decaying organic material from a landscape. Uses include forest management, ecological restoration, land clearing and wildfire fuel management. Burns are usually done in cooler months. Fire can stimulate germination of some trees, and in grassland it shifts species towards natives and removes invasives. Planning stresses safety, preventing escape and limiting smoke. Back burning against the wind gives a slower, controllable fire and a black line. Indigenous peoples use fire worldwide, and it has been used to clear land since the Neolithic. The risk is real: the Calf Canyon/Hermits Peak Fire, New Mexico's largest wildfire, began from two US Forest Service controlled burns that got out of control and merged.

nature-eco-713.title: The Forest Stewardship Council: certifying wood
nature-eco-713.text: Look for the FSC mark on paper or timber and you are seeing a market-based answer to {{ref:nature-eco-053}}. The Forest Stewardship Council is an international non-profit, multistakeholder organization founded in 1993 that promotes responsible forest management through timber certification. It runs a global certification system for forests and forest products. Members join one of three chambers: environmental, social and economic. Governments cannot be members and engage only as land owners. FSC does not audit itself. It accredits certification bodies, which then certify forests and companies to its standards. In September 2012 some 165 million hectares in 80 countries were certified, and about 24,000 chain of custody certificates were active in 107 countries. The main competing system is PEFC, criticized for little local or environmental organization influence and lack of transparency.
